title: Animations and Transitions
subtitle: Make Interfaces Feel Alive
description: Learn how to create smooth, professional interface interactions with CSS transitions, transforms, keyframe animations, timing functions, delays, animation controls and practical micro-interactions. Build animated buttons, cards, navigation, notifications, loading states and application components while learning how to use motion without making a website distracting or difficult to use.

blocks.text: Welcome to Animations and Transitions
You have already learned how to control the structure, appearance, spacing, layout and responsiveness of a website.
Now we are going to control how an interface changes.
This is where your CSS begins to feel much closer to a real application interface.
A good animation does not exist just to look beautiful.
It can tell the user that something changed, guide attention, confirm an action, or make an interface feel easier to understand.
Open your editor.
Create a file called index.html.
We are going to build one connected application interface throughout this lesson.

blocks.title: Card Interaction
blocks.output: The course card lifts, highlights its border and gains depth.

blocks.text: This is a useful example of a micro-interaction.
The movement is small because the goal is to communicate interaction, not distract the learner.
A professional interface often uses many small interactions instead of one huge animation.

blocks.question: A course card should feel clickable when hovered. Which combination gives the most controlled interaction?
options: transform, transition and a subtle shadow
large rotation, long animation and flashing colors
blocks.correctFeedback: Correct. Small coordinated changes communicate interaction without overwhelming the learner.
blocks.incorrectFeedback: Think about the purpose of a course card: it should communicate interaction, not become the main attraction.
blocks.reasoning: Professional micro-interactions usually use subtle transform, transition and depth changes.
blocks.hint: Choose the option that improves usability while staying subtle.

blocks.text: Transition Multiple Properties Carefully
Real components often change more than one property.
For example, a button can change its background, color, shadow and position.

blocks.title: Multiple Transitions
blocks.output: Several visual properties change smoothly together.

blocks.text: Notice that each property has its own duration and timing function.
You do not need to animate every property on an element.
Choose only the properties that help communicate the interaction.

blocks.question: A button changes color and moves upward on hover. Which transition setup directly supports both changes?
blocks.correctFeedback: Correct. Both properties are explicitly included in the transition.
blocks.incorrectFeedback: The transition list needs to include each property you want to animate.
blocks.reasoning: CSS can transition multiple properties by separating them with commas.
blocks.hint: Which two properties are actually changing?

blocks.text: When Transition Is Not Enough
Transitions are excellent when an element moves from one state to another.
But what if you want an animation to run automatically when the page loads?
That is where CSS animations and keyframes become useful.
A keyframe animation defines stages of an animation.

blocks.title: Your First Keyframes
blocks.output: The card gradually appears when the animation starts.

blocks.text: The @keyframes block describes the stages.
The animation property applies those stages to an element.
This is different from transition because the animation can run without waiting for a hover or focus change.

blocks.question: A notification should automatically fade into view when it appears. Which CSS feature is the better choice?
blocks.correctFeedback: Correct. Keyframes allow an animation to run through defined stages.
blocks.incorrectFeedback: This effect should happen automatically rather than requiring the user to hover.
blocks.reasoning: Keyframes define the animation stages, while animation applies the effect.
blocks.hint: You need the element to animate without a hover.

blocks.text: Understanding @keyframes
Keyframes can use from and to for simple animations.
They can also use percentages when you need more stages.

blocks.title: A Multi-Stage Animation
blocks.output: The badge grows slightly and returns to its original size repeatedly.

blocks.text: The 0 percent stage is the beginning.
The 50 percent stage happens halfway through.
The 100 percent stage is the end.
The infinite value makes the animation repeat.
Be careful with infinite animations because constant movement can distract users.

blocks.question: A status badge should gently grow and return to its normal size once. Which animation setup is more appropriate than an infinite loop?
blocks.correctFeedback: Correct. Without infinite, the animation runs once by default.
blocks.incorrectFeedback: The requirement says the animation should happen once.
blocks.reasoning: CSS animations normally run once unless an iteration count such as infinite is supplied.
blocks.hint: Remove the value that explicitly requests repetition.

blocks.text: Animation Duration, Delay and Iteration
CSS animations give you more control than simply choosing a duration.
You can control duration, timing function, delay, iteration count, direction and fill mode.

blocks.title: Animation Controls
blocks.output: The card waits briefly, fades in, runs once and keeps the appropriate animation state.

blocks.text: The animation shorthand can combine these settings.

blocks.title: Animation Shorthand
blocks.output: The shorthand represents the animation name, duration, timing, delay, iteration count and fill mode.

blocks.text: As projects become larger, understanding both the longhand properties and shorthand syntax will help you debug animations.

blocks.question: A page element should wait 0.5 seconds before its animation starts. Which property controls that waiting period?
blocks.correctFeedback: Correct. animation-delay controls when the animation begins.
blocks.incorrectFeedback: Look for the property that controls the waiting time before an animation starts.
blocks.reasoning: Duration controls how long the animation runs, while delay controls when it begins.
blocks.hint: The question is about waiting before starting.

blocks.text: Build a Loading Indicator
Loading states are common in real applications.
For example, a dashboard may need to show that information is being prepared.
Let's create a simple CSS loading indicator.

blocks.title: Loader HTML
blocks.output: An empty element will become the visual loader.

blocks.title: Loader Animation

blocks.text: The border creates the circular shape.
The keyframe rotates the element.
The infinite iteration keeps it moving until the loading state is removed.
This is a real application pattern you can reuse later.

blocks.question: Why does the loader use animation-iteration-count through the infinite value?
options: Because a loading indicator should repeat until the loading state ends
Because infinite makes the loader faster
Because infinite changes the border width
Because infinite is required for all CSS animations
blocks.correctFeedback: Correct. A loader may need to continue moving while the application is processing something.
blocks.incorrectFeedback: Think about what the loader represents: an ongoing process.
blocks.reasoning: The animation repeats while the application is in a loading state.
blocks.hint: The loading process may last longer than one animation cycle.

blocks.text: Build a Notification Animation
Notifications are another common application component.
A new notification can slide into view instead of suddenly appearing.

blocks.title: Notification Entrance
blocks.output: The notification smoothly enters from the side.

blocks.text: Notice that we animate both opacity and transform.
Combining two simple properties can create a much more natural entrance.
You can use the same thinking for menus, cards, dialogs and other interface components.

blocks.question: A notification should enter from the right while gradually becoming visible. Which pair of properties best represents that effect?
blocks.correctFeedback: Correct. Opacity controls visibility while transform can control the entrance movement.
blocks.incorrectFeedback: Think about one property for visibility and another for movement.
blocks.reasoning: Combining opacity with translateX creates a clean fade-and-slide effect.
blocks.hint: One property controls visibility; one controls position visually.

blocks.text: Navigation Micro-Interactions
Navigation is one of the most important places to use subtle interaction.
A navigation link can change color and show an underline when the user interacts with it.

blocks.title: Animated Navigation Link
blocks.output: The navigation text changes color and the underline grows smoothly.

blocks.text: This example combines pseudo-elements, pseudo-classes and transitions.
You already learned these concepts in the responsive design lesson.
Now you are combining them to create a professional interaction.

blocks.question: Why is focus-visible included alongside hover for the navigation interaction?
options: To make keyboard-focused links visibly interactive
To make the link load faster
To remove the underline on mobile
blocks.correctFeedback: Correct. Keyboard users also need a clear visual indication of focus.
blocks.incorrectFeedback: Think about users who navigate without a mouse.
blocks.reasoning: Accessible interfaces should communicate focus, not only mouse hover.
blocks.hint: Imagine navigating the page using the keyboard.

blocks.text: Animation Versus Transition
Let's make the difference very clear.
Use transition when you want a smooth change between states.
Hovering over a button is a classic example.
Use animation and keyframes when you need defined stages or an animation that can run independently.
A loading spinner is a classic example.

blocks.title: The Difference
blocks.output: Transition responds to a state change. Animation can run independently.

blocks.question: Which situation is the clearest example of using a transition instead of a keyframe animation?
options: A button smoothly changing color on hover
A logo bouncing three times when the page opens
A notification entering through multiple keyframe stages
blocks.correctFeedback: Correct. Hover creates a state change, which is exactly where transition is useful.
blocks.incorrectFeedback: Which option describes a simple before-and-after state change?
blocks.reasoning: Transitions are ideal for interactions such as hover, focus and other state changes.
blocks.hint: Look for the option that has a clear starting state and interactive ending state.

blocks.text: Build a Modal Entrance
Real applications often display dialogs or modal windows.
The CSS animation should support the user rather than make the modal difficult to read.

blocks.title: Modal Animation
blocks.output: The modal gently appears and settles into position.

blocks.text: Notice how small the movement is.
Professional UI animation is often about restraint.
The user should understand what happened instead of wondering why the entire screen is moving.

blocks.question: A login dialog should appear smoothly without distracting the user. Which animation style is the most appropriate?
options: A small fade with subtle movement
blocks.correctFeedback: Correct. A subtle entrance communicates that the dialog has appeared without distracting from the form.
blocks.incorrectFeedback: The goal is usability, not attention-seeking movement.
blocks.reasoning: Small opacity and transform changes are appropriate for dialog entrances.
blocks.hint: Choose the animation that helps the user notice the new element while keeping attention on its content.

blocks.text: Respect Reduced Motion
Not every user experiences motion in the same way.
Some users prefer reduced motion because large or frequent movement can be uncomfortable.
CSS provides a media feature that lets you respond to that preference.

blocks.title: Reduced Motion
blocks.output: Animations and transitions are greatly reduced for users who request reduced motion.

blocks.text: This is an important step toward professional and accessible CSS.
Animation is not only about visual design.
It is also about respecting the people using your application.

blocks.question: Why should a professional website consider prefers-reduced-motion?
options: To respect users who request less motion
To make every animation run forever
To force all users to disable animations
blocks.correctFeedback: Correct. The setting allows the interface to reduce motion according to the user's preference.
blocks.incorrectFeedback: Think about accessibility and user preferences.
blocks.reasoning: Reduced-motion preferences help make animated interfaces more comfortable and accessible.
blocks.hint: This is about the person using the interface.

blocks.text: Animation Performance
A beautiful animation is not useful if it makes the interface feel slow.
For many common interactions, transform and opacity are good properties to animate.
Be careful about constantly animating large areas of the page.
Avoid unnecessary animation on every element.
Animation should have a purpose.

blocks.title: A Better Micro-Interaction
blocks.output: A small, focused interaction using transform and opacity-related motion.

blocks.text: When you design a real application, always ask what the animation communicates.
If you cannot answer that question, the animation may not be necessary.

blocks.question: Which approach is more likely to produce a professional interface?
options: Use subtle motion where it communicates interaction or change
Make every button spin on hover
Use long animations for every page element
blocks.correctFeedback: Correct. Good animation has a purpose and supports the interface.
blocks.incorrectFeedback: Professional animation is usually intentional rather than constant.
blocks.reasoning: Purposeful motion helps users understand interaction and state changes without creating unnecessary distraction.
blocks.hint: Think about animation as communication, not decoration alone.

blocks.text: Animation Debugging
When an animation does not work, do not immediately rewrite everything.
First check whether the @keyframes name matches the animation name.
Then check whether the duration exists.
Then check whether the element actually receives the class or state that should trigger the effect.
Finally, inspect whether another CSS rule is overriding the property.

blocks.title: Find the Error
blocks.output: The animation does not run because slideIn does not match the defined slideUp keyframes.

blocks.text: The keyframe is called slideUp.
The animation is trying to use slideIn.
Those names must match.

blocks.title: Corrected Version
blocks.output: The animation now uses the correct keyframe name.

blocks.question: An animation is defined with @keyframes slideUp, but the element uses animation: slideIn 0.4s ease. What should you check first?
options: Whether the animation name matches the keyframe name
blocks.correctFeedback: Correct. The animation name must reference the defined keyframes.
blocks.incorrectFeedback: Compare the two names carefully.
blocks.reasoning: The browser needs the animation declaration to reference the actual @keyframes name.
blocks.hint: Read slideUp and slideIn carefully.

blocks.text: Stop and inspect what we just built.
The navigation uses transition.
The buttons use transform and transition.
The hero uses keyframes.
The cards use keyframes and hover transitions.
The layout uses Grid and Flexbox.
The typography responds using clamp.
The interface also respects reduced-motion preferences.
This is the level of thinking you will need for the final CSS project.
Your Animation Design Rules
Before we finish, remember these rules.
Use transition for smooth state changes.
Use transform for visual movement, scaling and rotation.
Use @keyframes for multi-stage or independent animations.
Keep interface motion short and purposeful.
Do not animate everything.
Test keyboard focus as well as mouse hover.
Respect prefers-reduced-motion.
Always ask what the animation communicates.
A professional developer does not add motion simply because CSS makes it possible.
A professional developer uses motion to improve the experience.
Final CSS Knowledge Check
This is your final knowledge check before the complete CSS project.
Do not choose an answer because it looks familiar.
Think like the developer who has to build the interface.

blocks.question: A dashboard button should smoothly change color when hovered. Which tool is most appropriate?
blocks.correctFeedback: Correct. Hover is a state change, making transition the natural choice.
blocks.incorrectFeedback: The effect is a smooth change between two states.
blocks.reasoning: Transition handles state changes such as hover and focus.
blocks.hint: No repeated or multi-stage animation is required.

blocks.question: A loader must rotate continuously while data is being prepared. Which approach is strongest?
blocks.correctFeedback: Correct. A repeating keyframe animation is appropriate for a loader.
blocks.incorrectFeedback: The loader needs to keep moving without a hover interaction.
blocks.reasoning: Keyframes can define rotation and infinite repeats the animation.
blocks.hint: Think about an animation that runs independently.

blocks.question: A card should rise 4px on hover without pushing neighboring cards downward. Which approach is best?
blocks.correctFeedback: Correct. Transform provides the visual movement without using layout spacing for the effect.
blocks.incorrectFeedback: Think about the transform feature used for visual movement.
blocks.reasoning: translateY is designed for moving an element visually.
blocks.hint: You learned this earlier in the lesson.

blocks.question: A notification should fade and slide into view when it appears. Which approach best matches the requirement?
blocks.correctFeedback: Correct. Keyframes can define the entrance stages using opacity and transform.
blocks.incorrectFeedback: The notification needs an independent entrance animation.
blocks.reasoning: Opacity controls visibility and transform controls the movement.
blocks.hint: The effect has multiple stages and should run when the notification appears.

blocks.question: A user prefers reduced motion. What should your CSS ideally do?
blocks.correctFeedback: Correct. Respecting reduced-motion preferences is part of accessible interface design.
blocks.incorrectFeedback: Think about accessibility and user comfort.
blocks.reasoning: The prefers-reduced-motion media feature allows the design to reduce motion for users who request it.
blocks.hint: The preference is specifically asking for less motion.

blocks.question: A developer has added ten different continuous animations to a dashboard. What is the best professional response?
options: Keep them all because animation is always better
Review each animation and keep only motion that has a useful purpose
blocks.correctFeedback: Correct. Professional motion should support the interface rather than overwhelm the user.
blocks.incorrectFeedback: More animation does not automatically mean a better interface.
blocks.reasoning: Animation should communicate state, interaction or hierarchy. Unnecessary motion can distract users.
blocks.hint: Ask what each animation communicates.

blocks.question: An animation does not run. The @keyframes block is called fadeUp, but the element says animation: fadeIn 0.5s ease. What is the likely problem?
options: The animation name does not match the keyframe name
blocks.correctFeedback: Correct. The animation declaration must reference the defined keyframes.
blocks.incorrectFeedback: Compare the names used in @keyframes and animation.
blocks.reasoning: fadeUp and fadeIn are different names, so the browser is not being told to use the defined animation.
blocks.hint: Compare fadeUp with fadeIn.

blocks.question: You are building a course platform. Which animation strategy is most professional for course cards?
options: Subtle lift and shadow on hover
blocks.correctFeedback: Correct. A subtle lift communicates that the card is interactive.
blocks.incorrectFeedback: Think about how a learner should experience a course dashboard.
blocks.reasoning: Small hover interactions improve discoverability without distracting from course content.
blocks.hint: Choose the interaction that supports the learner's task.

blocks.text: Final Challenge: Think Like a CSS Developer
Imagine you are building a real learning platform.
It has a navigation bar, dashboard cards, progress indicators, buttons, notifications and a loading state.
The interface must work on phones and larger screens.
Now decide what each CSS technique should do.

blocks.question: The dashboard cards should respond to hover, the loading indicator should rotate continuously, and a notification should slide in once. Which mapping is strongest?
options: Cards: transition, Loader: keyframes infinite, Notification: keyframes once
Cards: keyframes infinite, Loader: transition, Notification: margin
Cards: margin, Loader: hover transition, Notification: border
Cards: position fixed, Loader: Grid, Notification: Flexbox
blocks.correctFeedback: Excellent. You are now choosing CSS tools based on interface requirements.
blocks.incorrectFeedback: Match each requirement to the CSS feature designed for that behavior.
blocks.reasoning: Hover state changes are ideal for transitions, continuous loading uses repeating keyframes, and a one-time entrance uses keyframes without infinite repetition.
blocks.hint: Separate state changes from independent animations.

blocks.question: A professional developer notices that an animation looks impressive but makes the interface harder to use. What should happen next?
options: Make it faster and keep it regardless
Reduce or remove the animation if it does not improve the experience
blocks.correctFeedback: Exactly. Good CSS serves the user, not the other way around.
blocks.incorrectFeedback: Return to the main principle of this lesson: motion should have a purpose.
blocks.reasoning: A visually impressive effect is still a poor design choice if it hurts usability.
blocks.hint: Ask whether the animation helps the user.

blocks.text: Prepare for the Final CSS Project
You have now reached the final stage of the CSS foundation.
You know how selectors target elements.
You know how colors, borders and backgrounds create visual identity.
You understand the box model and how spacing affects real interfaces.
You understand typography.
You can build layouts with Flexbox.
You can build structured layouts with Grid.
You can make interfaces responsive.
You can use variables, positioning, pseudo-classes and pseudo-elements.
And now you can add purposeful interaction and motion.
But knowing CSS properties is not the final goal.
The final goal is being able to look at a design and build it.
That is exactly what Lesson 10 is about.
You will bring your CSS knowledge together to build a complete website.
The same thinking will later help you build complete application interfaces.
HTML gives your application structure.
CSS gives it visual identity, layout, responsiveness and interaction.
JavaScript will later give those interfaces behavior and logic.
Together, these skills move you toward building real websites and applications.
Lesson 9 Complete
Excellent work.
You have completed Animations and Transitions.
You can now create smooth state changes, visual transformations, keyframe animations, loading states, notifications and professional micro-interactions.
You also learned how to think about accessibility, performance and purposeful motion.
Do not think of these skills as separate CSS tricks.
Think of them as tools inside your interface-building toolbox.
In the final CSS lesson, you will use that toolbox to build.
Not just practice.
A complete website.
